v6 was by far the biggest set of changes, split into a stacked sequence of PRs:
lobe-ui#699
removed the antd components and
ThemeProvider
;
lobe-ui#700
dropped the antd, antd-style, and rc-* dependencies; and
lobe-ui#702
merged
src/base-ui
completely empty.
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
back into the root directory, getting rid of the base-ui subpath. With the coexistence phase over, we tore down that v5 scaffolding and exported the new components straight from the root entry. In early October, the downstream libraries first ported their own component usage over to base-ui (
lobe-editor#222
and
lobe-charts#32
), before each bumped to lobe-ui 6 and stripped out antd.
This cascade of changes couldn't be released and verified piecemeal. Instead, we tested across repos using pkg.pr.new preview packages: PRs for lobe-ui and the five downstream libraries each published preview packages, and
lobehub#20503
pointed all dependencies to those preview URLs. We compared lobe-chat against production page by page to ensure zero visual regressions before officially publishing in dependency order and and then switched back to real version numbers. PR #20503 alone updated imports across 2,728 files, purged antd from 24 workspace packages, and finally left
pnpm ls -r antd
with nothing to show.
Moving styles from runtime generation to build-time compilation
Dropping antd took care of components, but styles were still being generated at runtime. lobe-ui wrote its component styles in antd-style, built on Emotion: on page load, JavaScript generated CSS on the fly and inserted it into the page. The initial optimization pass replaced dynamic hooks with
createStaticStyles
, ensuring components no longer recomputed styles on every re-render. Yet the insertion step remained. In September,
lobehub#19066
pre-computed purely static calls at build time, slashing the time spent on styles during cold home page loads from ~56ms to ~28ms. The remaining ~14ms came from
insertRule
itself—an unavoidable cost as long as emotion was in the loop.
To eliminate this remaining overhead, styles needed to compile down to plain CSS files at build time. I chose StyleX, which splits styles into deduplicated atomic classes during compilation. The underlying mechanics—and how I migrated 10,000 lines of CSS to StyleX on another project—are covered in
"From Pure CSS to StyleX: Migrating 10,000 Lines of CSS with AI"
. For lobe-ui 6,
lobe-ui#701
piloted the approach on six components: Button, Divider, Spin, Switch, Tag, and Tooltip. Then
lobe-ui#705
migrated the remaining 89 modules in one go, freeing all 95 component modules from their emotion dependency. Markup not directly rendered by lobe-ui—such as Markdown, KaTeX, and code syntax highlighting—was styled with plain CSS in
@layer lobe-ui
.
Migrating 89 modules in a single pass succeeded thanks to per-element visual regression testing: we captured 500 demos in the documentation site across both light and dark themes while comparing computed styles for every element. Out of 1,000 runs, 891 matched completely. The remaining runs differed only because of animation timing, image loading, Mermaid layout jitter, or subpixel antialiasing differences. We also installed the packaged bundle into lobe-chat and ran the same comparison across 45 routes and 5 open menus.
Here are median cold-start metrics for the authenticated home page in lobe-chat, with CPU throttled 4x and each build tested across 8 runs. Both builds had already shed antd; the only difference was whether styles were generated at runtime via emotion or compiled ahead of time via StyleX:
Runtime overhead dropped across the board: document CSS rules fell from 5,817 to 4,429, blocking time decreased by 9%, and style recalculations dropped by 8%. The downside was First Contentful Paint: 4G FCP climbed from 440ms to 594ms because lobe-ui's
style.css
bundled styles for all 95 components, weighing in at 179KB uncompressed. In lobe-chat, it ended up in the single render-blocking stylesheet, pushing initial blocking CSS from 20.2KB to 45.5KB (gzipped). On November 2,
lobe-ui#776
introduced the fix: per-component stylesheets, so applications only pull in what they use. In a benchmark app using 30 components, per-component loading yielded 45.9KB, compared to 59.5KB for the full
style.css
bundle. lobe-chat is currently still running on the monolithic
style.css
and hasn't made the switch yet.
What antd was doing behind the scenes
Once antd and emotion were completely removed from the dependency tree, hidden assumptions began surfacing. Beyond providing components, antd silently did plenty of heavy lifting for the entire page: setting root fonts and sizes, providing baseline icon layout, and supplying a global reset. None of this was ever stated in application code—it only became visible after antd was removed:

, leaving

alone so rem values don't change; see
lobe-ui#703

.anticon

inline-flex
and

lobe-ui#705

shorthand into longhand lost

along with other properties only reset by the shorthand

; see also lobe-ui#705

stops hiding scrollbars

@layer lobe-ui
, the app's unlayered

rule took higher priority

lobe-ui
in the cascade
The last two issues both trace back to CSS cascade layers. Placing component styles into
@layer
, the layer hierarchy (from lowest to highest) looked like this:
Unlayered styles always beat layered styles, regardless of selector specificity. That makes overriding component styles easy, but, an offhand global rule in application code can also quietly stomp over components.
The icon vertical misalignment was the trickiest to catch. The visual regression tool mentioned in lobe-ui#705 used the v6 preview as its baseline. But
.anticon
styles had vanished earlier when
lobe-ui#699
stripped antd, so the regression was already baked into the baseline, leaving the diff completely empty. We eventually caught it with the naked eye in the Tree component. Once we added a visual comparison against an antd-era lobe-chat build, vertical alignment across 73 icons and text elements snapped into place on the home page, appearance settings, and community page—where the pre-fix preview had matched only 3. A visual regression baseline must be the last version users actually saw, not the previous commit.
Conversely, bugs in the old implementation could also sneak into the baseline. emotion's
cx
merges multiple class names into one, which prevented the
& + &
divider rule in lobe-chat's workspace empty state from matching any element. After the move to StyleX, it kicked in for the first time, and the comparison tool flagged it as a diff. We kept this change as intended behavior.
How much lighter is a Button after dropping antd?
Because application code in the main lobe-chat bundle was also evolving over the year, comparing it before and after wouldn't isolate what changed in the component library itself. Instead, I spun up a clean Vite project rendering a single Button, building it with v5 (5.64.4, with the antd Button) and v6 (6.15.0). Both setups included only what was strictly necessary for rendering: v5 wrapped the button in
ThemeProvider
, while v6 imported
theme.css
alongside the Button stylesheet, plus a
MotionProvider
.
Excluding React, Button-related JS dropped from ~130KB to ~32KB. The bulk of v5 came from antd and its rc-component dependencies, totaling around 287KB uncompressed; v6's 32KB mostly belongs to the motion animation library, with lobe-ui itself accounting for just ~9KB uncompressed. The tradeoff is that v6 introduces a static CSS file measuring 22.6KB gzipped, of which 16.5KB is "}
theme.css
design tokens, shared across all components; v5 shipped no CSS files because JavaScript generated styles at runtime, shared across all components and generated styles at runtime with JS.
During benchmarking, we also uncovered an issue: importing from the root entry
import { Button } from '@lobehub/ui'
, both versions pulled in around 450KB of unminified —or roughly 141KB gzipped KaTeX and Markdown parsing code that had nothing to do with Button. The figures above already exclude this overhead. In v6, importing from the
es/Button
subpath avoids pulling it in entirely, whereas v5 only exported the root entry, leaving no way around it. The reason was that the root entry re-exported
@lobehub/streamdown
's
rehypeStreamAnimated
, but streamdown's package.json didn't declare
sideEffects
, and the module top level contained impure
memo()
calls and
displayName
assignments. Because bundlers couldn't prove they were side-effect-free, they had to keep the entire Markdown rendering stack. The fix was shipped in
lobehub/streamdown#7
in version 1.4.5, simply adding to package.json:
"sideEffects": false
. lobe-ui 6's dependency range automatically picks up this new release. After a clean reinstall, importing from the root entry matches the subpath import at 92.4KB.
Beyond bundle size, we also eliminated the leftover styling overhead from antd. The share, workbench, and auth SSR apps previously had to extract antd's static CSS separately;
lobehub#20503
deleted that entire pipeline. We also removed the
antdOverride
global stylesheet that existed solely to override antd defaults, while
lobehub#21046
purged the application CSS rules written for
.ant-*
classes, which no longer match any elements once antd was removed.
Next step: can we migrate Application Code to StyleX in One Go?
With the component library migrated, styling in application code was still using the legacy styling approach: using
createStaticStyles
at the top of a file to write CSS in template strings, which Emotion then injected into the page at runtime. On canary, 1,112 files still follow this pattern, while around 350 have been converted to StyleX. On October 20,
lobehub#21042
paved the way for writing StyleX in application code, allowing direct imports of lobe-ui design tokens. Below is a file from the homepage sidebar notifications list, shown before and after the rewrite in
lobehub#21446
:
Before:
createStaticStyles
CodeBlock Loading...
After: StyleX
CodeBlock Loading...
Rewriting a single file isn't hard; the hard part is proving it looks identical afterward. Notice the extra property on the right:
backgroundImage: 'none'
on the right: the original
background
is a shorthand property that also resets the background image. StyleX discourages shorthand properties, which means writing only
backgroundColor
drops that reset. The
font: inherit
pitfall in the earlier table stems from the exact same issue. Visual differences like this rarely show up in screenshots, and comparing over a thousand files by eye is painfully slow and error-prone. Beyond writing a migrator, we needed an automated tool to confirm styles stayed identical before and after the rewrite and catch pitfalls like the ones above before and after.
Our initial plan was to compare computed styles rather than screenshots: checking browser-computed styles before and after across themes, breakpoints, and hover or focus states for every styled element. Taking HomeSidebar (
lobehub#21446
) and ChatInput (
lobehub#21452
), it caught an actual regression:
Params/Controls.tsx
had its
font: inherit
expanded into longhands, causing the button to lose its
font-feature-settings
. The exact trap we stumbled into in the component library resurfaced during the app migration—except this time the tool caught it first.
Before trusting the tool when it reported "equivalent," we had to prove the tool itself was trustworthy. That verification baseline required three things: tell noise from real differences by remaining completely stable when comparing a version against itself; catch actual regressions by flagging 100% of intentionally injected changes; and know its limits by deferring anything synthetic rendering can't cover to human review, storing those sign-offs with the source code and invalidating them whenever the code changes.
Once the baseline was locked in, we re-ran all 16 migration PRs summarized in
lobehub#22041
. The results fell into three buckets: proven equivalent and passed immediately, divergent and sent back for fixes, or unprovable and escalated for human review.
To save reviewers from digging through logs, I built a local reporting UI. The overview lists results by file and condition, letting you click into any element to inspect evidence and see a side-by-side live comparison. Meanwhile, the sign-off page groups items by root cause for batch approval.
Report overview: one row per file, one column per condition. ✓ indicates equivalent; numbers show counts of differing elements.
Sign-off view: grouped by reason, with side-by-side renders comparing before and after under the same condition
Summary
Between December 2025 and October 2026, lobe-ui evolved from v3 to v6, direct antd imports in lobe-chat dropped from a peak of 485 files to zero, and the JS footprint for a single Button shrank from around 130KB to roughly 32KB (gzipped). Looking back, once AI and codemods made rewriting code cheap, the real bottlenecks came down to two challenges: creating coexistence mechanisms and guardrails so shipping never stopped while legacy patterns continuously shrank, and automatically proving with tooling that behavior and styles hadn't regressed. A few key practices from this year transfer well to other projects:
Let new and legacy components coexist in the same package, migrating component by component.
v5's
base-ui
subpath spared application code from an all-or-nothing rewrite, allowing us to tear down that scaffolding in v6.
Migrate the highest-overhead, most interconnected layer first.
Overlays share positioning and z-index logic. Declarative modals stay mounted all the time, whereas an imperative approach only incurs overhead when a modal actually opens.
Make new components drop-in replacements.
Match both the API and visual appearance of legacy components so app code only changes import paths, porting over quirks like Tag's color resolution verbatim.
Lock down migrated categories with lint rules, grandfathering existing usage via allowlists.
AGENTS.md
and skills couldn't prevent AI agents from mimicking legacy antd patterns found in existing files. Import counts only began to steadily decline once we added lint rules and commit hooks on June 26.
Verify equivalence via computed styles, using the version users actually see as the baseline.
.anticon
positioning drift and
font: inherit
attribute loss both slipped past screenshot diffs and "compare against previous version" checks.
Isolate variables when measuring gains.
Instead of benchmarking entire production bundles, spin up a dedicated project rendering only a single Button—which also uncovered our root entry tree-shaking bug.

items.text: denizhalil-blogs published: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-116366 ClickHouse Server – Brotli v1.2.0 Decoder DoS/OOB-Write
items.title: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-116366 ClickHouse Server – Brotli v1.2.0 Decoder DoS/OOB-Write
items.content:
Introduction
ClickHouse is a widely deployed, high-performance columnar database management system designed for online analytical processing (OLAP). To maintain its exceptional read and write speeds, ClickHouse relies heavily on efficient data compression algorithms, including Google’s Brotli library. CVE-2026-116366 represents a critical security flaw in how ClickHouse handles incoming Brotli-compressed payloads. This vulnerability exposes affected servers to unauthenticated Remote Code Execution (RCE) and Denial of Service (DoS) attacks via memory corruption. As data architectures increasingly expose ingestion endpoints to wider networks for real-time analytics, vulnerabilities at the transport and decompression layers become highly attractive targets. Threat actors actively scan for exposed ClickHouse instances to exploit these low-level memory handling errors, bypassing application-level security controls entirely.
Learning Objectives
By the end of this analysis, readers will be able to:
Understand the core components and origins of CVE-2026-116366.
Analyze the technical mechanics of the Out-Of-Bounds (OOB) write vulnerability within the Brotli decoder.
Identify the specific attack vectors and network ports exploited by threat actors.
Determine if their infrastructure, including embedded analytics stacks, is running vulnerable software.
Apply appropriate remediation and network segmentation strategies to secure ClickHouse deployments.
What is ClickHouse Server – Brotli v1.2.0 Decoder DoS/OOB-Write (CVE-2026-116366)
CVE-2026-116366 is a critical vulnerability (CVSS 9.5) specific to ClickHouse Server, stemming from an underlying flaw in the bundled Google Brotli compression library (tracked upstream as CVE-2026-111497). Because ClickHouse natively accepts compressed data over its network interfaces to optimize data ingestion rates and reduce bandwidth, it routinely passes external, untrusted data streams directly to the Brotli C decoder. The core of the issue manifests when an unauthenticated attacker sends a maliciously crafted, Brotli-compressed payload directly to the ClickHouse server’s listening ports. Upon decompression, an out-of-bounds (OOB) write occurs, severely corrupting server memory. This corruption reliably results in an immediate crash of the ClickHouse daemon, creating a catastrophic Denial of Service (DoS) condition for data pipelines. Beyond simple service disruption, highly sophisticated threat actors can manipulate this heap memory corruption to achieve arbitrary code execution. By carefully structuring the out-of-bounds write to overwrite critical function pointers or execution flows, the attacker gains the ability to run malicious commands with the full operating system privileges of the ClickHouse database process, leading to total server compromise.
CVSS Severity:
9.5 (Critical) reflecting the lack of authentication required.
Attack Vector:
Network-based exploitation targeting default database ingestion ports.
Underlying Flaw:
Inherited directly from Google’s Brotli C library versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0.
Primary Impacts:
Denial of Service (DoS) via process crash and unauthenticated Remote Code Execution (RCE).
[Attacker] --(Crafted Brotli Payload)--> [Network Port 8123/9000]
|
v
[ClickHouse Ingestion Layer]
|
v
[Brotli C Decoder Module]
|
v
[Out-of-Bounds Memory Write]
|
+------------+------------+
| |
v v
[Process Crash (DoS)] [Remote Code Execution]
Technical Detail: How the Vulnerability Works
The root cause of this memory corruption lies within the C implementation of the Brotli decoder, specifically localized to the
DecodeBlockTypeAndLength()
function found within the
c/dec/decode.c
source file. When the Brotli decoder processes an incoming stream, it relies heavily on block switches to accurately manage different data types and their corresponding lengths. The vulnerability is explicitly triggered when this function encounters a malformed or structurally invalid block switch designed by an attacker. Instead of safely terminating the decoding process or throwing a handled exception upon encountering this invalid structure, the function yields an ambiguous return value. The critical failure occurs because the Brotli fast decoding path aggressively prioritizes speed and fails to validate this anomalous state. As the decoder continues processing the payload under demonstrably false assumptions about block lengths and boundary limits, it blindly writes the decompressed output.
Consequently, the decoder writes this output directly past the strictly enforced boundaries of its allocated heap memory buffer. In the context of ClickHouse, this OOB write is exceptionally dangerous because the decompression occurs synchronously as data streams in from the network interfaces. An attacker exploits this by simply delivering the payload over the default HTTP (8123) or Native (9000) ports before the database ever attempts to parse the content as a legitimate SQL query.
Vulnerable Function:
DecodeBlockTypeAndLength()
located within
c/dec/decode.c
.
Trigger Mechanism:
Intentional injection of malformed block switches within the compressed HTTP/TCP stream.
Validation Failure:
The fast decoding path ignores ambiguous return values from the underlying block parser.
Exploitation Phase:
Memory overwrite occurs during synchronous network stream decompression prior to SQL parsing.
Affected Software & Plugins
The vulnerability directly impacts self-hosted environments running ClickHouse Server versions that statically or dynamically bundle Brotli library versions ranging from 1.0.3 through 1.2.0. Because ClickHouse is heavily integrated into modern data architectures, the attack surface extends beyond standalone database clusters. Administrators must account for bare-metal, containerized, and orchestrated Kubernetes deployments running older, unpatched releases of the database software. Furthermore, organizations are frequently exposed unknowingly if they operate self-hosted software platforms that silently bundle ClickHouse as their underlying telemetry, logging, or data storage backend. Many open-source analytics stacks provide default deployment configurations that pull vulnerable ClickHouse container images, meaning security teams must audit their entire application dependency chain, not just the primary database servers.
Standalone Deployments:
Bare-metal servers and Docker/Kubernetes clusters running unpatched ClickHouse builds.
Embedded Analytics:
Self-hosted platforms like Langfuse, Plausible Analytics, or PostHog that utilize bundled ClickHouse containers.
Monitoring Stacks:
Self-hosted Sentry or custom observability pipelines utilizing ClickHouse for extensive log aggregation.
Client Applications:
Data processing drivers that ingest heavily compressed upstream data, potentially exposing client-side decoders.
Conclusion
CVE-2026-116366 emphatically highlights the persistent and systemic danger of memory safety vulnerabilities lurking within foundational C/C++ compression libraries. When these low-level libraries are integrated into high-performance, network-facing applications like ClickHouse, the security implications are magnified drastically. The CVSS score of 9.5 accurately reflects the severity of this threat, given that exploitation requires zero authentication and directly targets the default, often exposed, network ingestion ports. Immediate and comprehensive remediation requires upgrading ClickHouse to a fully patched release, such as version
26.3.62.3-lts
or the latest stable iterative build provided by the vendor. Security and operations teams must prioritize these upgrades across all environments, ensuring that embedded analytics containers and third-party dashboards relying on ClickHouse are also rebuilt with secure images. Relying solely on perimeter defenses is insufficient if internal threat actors or lateral movement capabilities exist within the corporate network. In the interim, or in environments where immediate patching is operationally unfeasible, administrators must enforce strict network segmentation protocols. Database ports should be bound exclusively to localhost (
127.0.0.1
) or highly restricted internal VPC subnets. Implementing aggressive firewall rules to unconditionally block public internet access to ports 8123, 8443, 9000, and 9440 is a mandatory defensive posture to mitigate external exploitation attempts until patches are permanently applied.

items.title: Two weeks on: what happened to October's critical vulnerabilities
items.content:
Between 16 and 23 October, five major security incidents went public in a single week: two remote code execution bugs in PHP, a memory corruption bug in Google’s Brotli decoder, a chain of four bugs in Plex Media Server, a CVSS 10.0 bug in GitLab, and eight compromised certificate authority keys at eMudhra.
Now that the month is over, here’s what happened next.
At a glance
Issue
Patch / containment
Exploitation
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
21 Oct
Attempt seen 17 Oct, before disclosure; CISA-listed 26 Oct; 24 PAN-OS firewalls rooted (Dream Research)
HTTP2Shell / Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497)
21 Oct
CISA-listed as exploited 27 Oct; public details of compromises limited. ELLIO’s documented attempt failed in lab replays
Plex2Shell (four CVEs)
Early Aug
CISA-listed 20 Oct; active exploitation confirmed by Plex: crypto miners, proxy malware
GitLab (CVE-2026-110264)
21 Oct
No public exploitation reported
GitLab (CVE-2026-97229, earlier flaw)
12 Oct
Exploitation attempts detected by GitLab; Alpine Linux targeted 20–21 Oct; CISA cites ongoing attacks
eMudhra CA keys
17 Oct (blocked)
No malicious use confirmed
PHP2Shell
Fixed:
21 October, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Who is affected and how to check:
PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCE (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
.
Exploited:
yes.
Amazon Threat Intelligence
recorded an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypots on 17 October, four days before public disclosure, and says it’s unclear how the actor got the exploit details that early. After disclosure, AWS reports broad exploitation attempts in the wild. CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 26 October.
Palo Alto Networks’ advisory
now says active exploitation has been observed against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. On 26 October,
Dream Research reported a campaign
that chained PHP2Shell with Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a Linux kernel privilege-escalation bug, and rooted 24 PAN-OS firewalls in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, plus an internal management server. Two of the firewalls belonged to a US government-affiliated organisation.
Unit 42 says
it independently verified the attacker’s tooling and the reported results. Dream Research found signs of AI-assisted tooling on the attacker’s infrastructure, but says it has no direct evidence AI wrote the exploit.
PHP2Shell is a blind remote memory corruption bug. A proof of concept built for one target rarely works on the next one, because memory layout depends on the PHP build, the extensions loaded and the application in front of it. Code execution needs an exploit tuned to each target.
That doesn’t make the bug overhyped. Attempts are widespread; confirmed successful compromises are much rarer.
Wiz says
it hasn’t seen a successful end-to-end PHP2Shell exploit in its own telemetry.
research
benchmark
php2shell: The exploitability gap between frontier and open models
We measured how long that adaptation takes: frontier models ported the exploit to a new target in hours, while the open models we tested didn't get there. That gap is likely to narrow.
Read the post
A separate PHP issue is still open. On 23 October,
PHP published an advisory
for CVE-2026-115560, another possible remote code execution path through session upload progress. It needs an unusual configuration: a non-default session serializer in server settings that the application switches back at runtime with
ini_set()
before
session_start()
. The 21 October releases don’t fix it, and no fix release is out yet. PHP’s mitigation for affected configurations is to set
session.upload_progress.enabled=0
at the server level. No exploitation has been reported.
The attacks a vendor has confirmed so far are against firewall management interfaces. Most people don’t think of their firewall as a PHP server, but its management interface runs PHP under the hood.
HTTP2Shell / Node2Shell (Brotli)
Fixed:
21 October, in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10, and in Node.js 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4. Fixes are still landing in software that bundles its own copy of Brotli. Linux distributions may backport the fix under older-looking version numbers, so check your distro’s security tracker rather than the version string alone.
Exploited:
CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 October, citing evidence of active exploitation. Public details of successful compromises remain limited.
On 26 October, threat-intelligence firm
ELLIO documented an exploitation attempt
involving a Brotli-compressed request targeting Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64. When ELLIO replayed the attacker’s chain in its lab, the final stage failed in all 50 attempts. The same source IP had been associated with PHP2Shell activity in OffSeq’s honeypots the week before.
The bug isn’t limited to Node.js. On 25 October,
Microsoft shipped out-of-band .NET updates
(8.0.33, 9.0.22 and 10.0.14) for the same flaw in .NET’s use of Brotli; request and automatic response decompression are off by default, and self-contained apps and containers carry their own runtime, so they need rebuilding. On 28 October,
AWS published a bulletin
saying its .NET and Node.js Lambda runtimes are affected, along with App Runner, CodeBuild curated images and other services. Updated Lambda container base images are already available. For functions deployed as ZIP files, AWS rolled out runtime updates in phases, scheduled to finish by 30 October for Node.js and 31 October for .NET, so check that your functions picked up the update. A real code or configuration change picks up the patched runtime sooner once it’s available in your region; AWS notes that “a zero-change update is not sufficient.”
Brotli is hard to fingerprint from the outside. A server doesn’t announce which decoder it uses, and the bug only matters if something decodes attacker-controlled Brotli data: request bodies, or responses fetched from a server the attacker controls.
We covered the bug and the exploit path in more detail in
Node2Shell: Brotli Decoder RCE in Node.js (CVE-2026-111497)
.
Plex2Shell
Fixed:
Plex fixed the issue in version 1.43.3.10861, released in early August.
Exploited:
yes, from about a day after the 16 October write-up.
A researcher’s honeypot recorded attacks
on 17 October that installed an XMRig-based crypto miner and proxy software, and Plex has confirmed active exploitation. No one has published a count of compromised servers. CISA added all four CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 20 October.
This is the only one of the five where the fix was out for more than two months before the attacks. Plex Media Server mostly runs on home and small-office machines, often exposed for remote streaming, and often not updated until something breaks.
GitLab (CVE-2026-110264)
Fixed:
21 October, in 19.5.1, 19.4.3 and 19.3.6, with backports to four older branches. GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were patched before disclosure.
Exploited:
no public exploitation reported for this flaw. The bug was in the Ruby regular expression engine GitLab ships, not in GitLab’s own code.
An earlier GitLab flaw in the same family is under attack.
GitLab says it has detected exploitation attempts
against CVE-2026-97229, fixed on 12 October, and has published detection rules. Shadowserver tracks nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it hasn’t said how many are patched.
The best-documented case is
Alpine Linux
, whose GitLab instance was targeted on 20 and 21 October. Alpine found no evidence the attacker succeeded but couldn’t rule it out, so it rebuilt the instance, reset all passwords and replaced GitLab’s secret keys. Alpine had two patching misses. Before the attack, it upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of the patched 19.3.5 by mistake. Then its upgrade to 19.3.6 on 22 October, after the attempts, still didn’t close the path: the fix is a patch to Ruby that GitLab only applies in its official packages, and Alpine’s image used standard Ruby.
If you self-host GitLab and haven’t upgraded, do it now. A successful exploit could expose repositories and CI/CD secrets accessible to the GitLab service account.
eMudhra
Fixed:
Chrome blocked the eight affected keys within two hours of the 17 October report, and other browsers and runtimes followed. Chrome stopped trusting the affected eMudhra root certificate on 27 October.
Exploited:
no public exploitation reported.
Google says
no website certificates from the affected intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency logs before the block, and
eMudhra says
it isn’t aware of any evidence the weak keys were recovered or exploited before disclosure. eMudhra’s board decided on 22 October to leave the global TLS certificate business.
If you have certificates chained to the eMudhra root, they need replacing with another CA.
Is there a pattern?
The PHP2Shell attacks a vendor has confirmed are on firewall appliances. Plex2Shell’s are self-hosted media servers with a fix from two months prior. ELLIO’s publicly documented Brotli exploit attempt was built for a specific Node.js build. In each case, the vulnerable code sits inside something people don’t think of as theirs to patch such as a vendor’s appliance, a bundled runtime, or a container base image.
Those are also the copies a version scan tends to miss. Brotli is compiled into runtimes and libraries that don’t list it as a dependency. GitLab’s fixes are in the Ruby it ships, which is why Alpine’s upgraded instance stayed vulnerable. And as of 28 October,
the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre
was tracking 757 products for PHP2Shell, with 218 confirmed vulnerable, 144 fixed and 354 still under investigation.
A patch existing doesn’t mean systems are patched.
Wiz’s telemetry
shows the number of internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell fell about 67% in the first week, but nearly half of the organisations originally affected were still vulnerable a week after disclosure. The remaining risk is in the copies you may not have realised you need to update. Check what’s actually running across your environment, and look for signs of exploitation that may have happened before you patched.

It's already been over two weeks since my last recap, so it's time to catch up on what's been happening lately.
Nyatabi Hits the App Store
Last time, I mentioned running into so many headaches after a trip that I decided to build an app. At the end of my last post, I wrote, "Musubicho is still in development and not finished yet." Less than two weeks later, I renamed it Nyatabi (喵旅) and officially launched it on the App Store. That said, I haven't even been the first one to really test it out in the wild. I'm such a homebody that even though a trip sparked the project, I haven't had the chance to use all its features myself yet. I just love building products—created purely out of passion.
It's live on the App Store now, and I put together a decent landing page for it. Feel free to check it out! (Though it's iOS-only for now.)
Nyatabi — your AI travel companion for iPhone
Plan with Musubi, explore together, split spending fairly and turn your route into memories. Your whole journey, in one local-first iPhone app.
Nyatabi
Beyond helping you map out trips, it lets an agent handle expense tracking and bill splitting on the go (either by snapping receipts or just telling it what you spent). In group chats, the agent can scout nearby restaurants or pull up your friends' locations. And once the trip wraps up, you can replay your route, generate an auto-edited highlight video, or export a detailed travel footprint report.
Before the official release, I shot a 4-part short video series walking through the entire flow: pre-trip planning → snapping receipts to split expenses on the go → settling balances with minimum transfers → everyday roommate bookkeeping. On October 16, I posted a full 2-minute demo.
Along the way, I also open-sourced the rounded-line icon set used in Nyatabi at
icons.nyatabi.app
.
Engineering shortcuts vs. engineering rigor: refusing to be a human test runner, I wired up XCUITest across two physical iPhones so agents could handle the entire closed loop of "implement → verify → fail → fix" on their own (check out my technical post, "
My AI-Native iOS Development & Verification Workflow
", for details).
It could be handy whether you're traveling or just going about everyday life: I've always found life-logging footprint apps a bit awkward to use, so I baked my own footprint features right in to track daily routines as well. I don't want to turn this into a full-on product pitch, so I'll stop here. If you're interested, feel free to give it a spin.

Download Nyatabi: AI Travel Planner by Moeru AI on the App Store. See screenshots, ratings and reviews, user tips, and more apps like Nyatabi: AI Travel Planner…

AI in the Trenches
A Love-Hate Relationship with Claude
I had a backup Claude alt account that managed to hold out for over two weeks, so I decided to upgrade it. Went from Pro to Max, only to get slapped with an instant ban—no refund, either. I was so anxious that night that I stayed up by myself until 5 a.m. Eventually, I couldn't help setting up yet another account, and that one's somehow still alive.
On top of that, my $DRAM shares kept tumbling before I could break even, so those days felt like a brutal double blow from Anthropic and $DRAM. It also got me calculating the real cost of compute inflation: last year, a $20 Claude subscription felt like it could do so much; now, even the $200 Max tier barely scratches the surface. By comparison, Apple's $99/year developer membership is so cheap it's almost moving.
OpenAI's "God Tier" Account and Kimi Falling Flat on Its Face
There was a funny little detour along the way. Around the 20th, I noticed a bug in OpenAI: an old 20x subscription was still usable even after downgrading or canceling. I honestly thought I'd struck gold with some chosen "god-tier" account. But by day five of freeloading, the bug got patched and my quota went straight to zero.
Then on the 23rd, I dropped $19 on Kimi, wanting to see how it compared to $20 Claude. I asked it to write a website footer—and before it even finished, barely ten minutes in, I slammed right into a 5-hour rate limit. Might as well just call yourselves QueueShot AI. When it comes to domestic models, everyone should just use DeepSeek—what are the rest of these garbage knockoffs even doing? DeepSeek is the only one that can actually play: no token sales, no bullshit. The API pricing is right there: take it or leave it. The TPS is right there too—DeepSeek 4.1 Flash pushes over 200 TPS, and at those prices, burn through as much as you want.
Unlike Kimi—their greed this time is honestly shameless: zero compute power, but pulling that classic Lei Jun artificial scarcity playbook and taking users for fools to the extreme.
Ryugi (流儀) — Open-Source Claude Artifacts
After getting jerked around like that, I thought: why not just build my own version of Claude Artifacts? I genuinely love using that feature. For docs, artboard designs, and architecture sketches, it's just so damn good—a product genuinely made with care.
But being locked into Claude's proprietary subscription was a dealbreaker. So what choice did I have? Build it myself.
Claude Artifacts support five types, and the ones I use most are Artboard, Document, and HTML. Sick of taking Anthropic's nonsense, I cobbled together a standalone workbench called "Ryugi" (
ryugi.innei.dev
).
Building this brought an unexpected bonus too: it completely changed my view of Codex's design skills. I used to think Codex was garbage at design, and just on the 10th I had tweeted about how miserable it was trying to write UI with it. But once I plugged it into Ryugi's Artboard workflow, it turned out to be surprisingly solid—I guess I was just using it wrong before. To my surprise, that tweet blew up, racking up 93K impressions and over 700 bookmarks.
I've been using it for a few days now, putting it through heavy daily use and constantly refining it. The cloud environment is live too, so now it helps me brainstorm, work on designs, hash out architecture docs, and even knock out small feature requests on the side.
The experience genuinely captures the vibe of Claude Artifacts now. Hooking this workflow up to other harnesses—like DeepSeek or Codex—makes them dramatically more useful. If you haven't tried it yet, you really should.

LobeHub Bids Farewell to AntD
On the work front: I've been here for almost a year now. Back when I first joined, I declared that I was going to ditch AntD once and for all. That turned into a ten-month marathon, but on the 9th of this month, I finally pulled it off—migrating everything over to
@base_ui
+
StyleX
(meaning
lobe-ui
v6).
Looking back at the numbers, the engineering scale was pretty wild:
lobe-ui
rewrote 54 components on top of Base UI, and AntD dependencies in
lobe-editor
,
lobe-charts
, and
lobe-icons
were completely eliminated.
The main repo has over 11,000 TypeScript files. Replacing the underlying component library spanned 28 PRs and touched 3,242 files, with the single largest PR modifying 1,040 files.
Along the way, we also migrated our CSS-in-JS setup to StyleX, slashing the original 179 emotion files down to just 3. The most satisfying part was running 5 agents across parallel branches: in three and a half hours, they plowed through 84 commits. We then ran regression tests across 45 routes using 1,000 screenshot comparisons and computed-style diffs, reliably catching 4 regressions.
Getting rid of AntD paid off right away. Bundle sizes shrank dramatically, and pages feel noticeably snappier. Thinking back, before AI agents existed, a core refactor of this scale would have easily taken an entire team a full quarter of grinding. But with today's models being so capable, I managed to knock out this massive project almost entirely on my own.
The Story Ends Here
Throughout October, blind dates from family and friends were nonstop, but most of the time chatting was pretty draining. Earlier in the month, I tweeted a rant saying some WeChat chats feel like "an LLM running on a potato server, taking hours of inference just to spit out a few characters, and if you don't send a request, you'll never get a response." That tweet unexpectedly racked up over 70,000 views, and predictably enough, I got hit with the "you're a nice guy" card in real life soon after.
But just a few days later, through another blind date, I unexpectedly met someone I could genuinely click with—something that hadn't happened in a long time.
I find myself wanting deeper conversations lately—talking about fundamental values, life outlooks, and thoughts on the future. In day-to-day life, finding someone who can actually match that energy is rare. But that night—which also happened to be our last conversation—we talked about so much. Beyond having plenty of shared interests, what hit hardest was a real resonance in who we are deep down. Just knowing someone on that exact same wavelength actually exists was a wonderful, lucky surprise.
Unfortunately, she felt our personalities were just too similar to be a good match. In the end, we parted ways gracefully, and that was where the story ended.
Turning My Resume into a Canvas
Another project I spent a lot of time on was completely rebuilding my personal resume page for Programmer's Day on October 24, launching it at

.
The spark was simple: surfing online recently, I saw a few personal sites and resumes that looked amazing, so I wanted to bring my own ideas into the mix and polish up something of my own. A traditional single-page format can't hold very much, so I turned it into a canvas you can freely pan, zoom, and explore—connecting all the projects I've worked on and milestones I've reached over the six or seven years since college into one continuous timeline.
Working on this canvas also ended up unlocking some new skills. To give the page some fitting background music, I dove into arranging with realistic virtual instruments, tweaking synthesis, and fine-tuning the details (huge thanks to
@wibus_wee
for walking me through Ozone mastering), and I even built an interactive sheet music display into the canvas.
Cramming a bunch of music arrangement and audio mastering just to build a resume was an unexpected bonus. Once I get around to picking music theory back up properly, I really should build an app for instruments and music theory.
